description: We are data scientists fascinated by the vastness of space and everything it has to offer. We are participating in this event to apply our knowledge, explore new challenges, and contribute our own small drop to this incredible community.

details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Time Viewer turns NASA’s all-sky near-infrared survey into something you can watch. You type coordinates — decimal degrees or sexagesimal — or pick one of four example targets, and that patch of sky plays back as a movie in time. You choose a detector and one of 102 spectral bands, step through every date SPHEREx visited that position, subtract two epochs to reveal what moved, inspect the quality masks, download the original FITS, and extract a spectrum and a light curve. Any view can be shared as a URL that restores it exactly.

It works in five stages. Coordinates are resolved to ICRS and, for known targets, corrected for proper motion to the date of each exposure. Queries go to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) and cutouts are centered on that position. A pure-science core aligns frames, decodes the FLAGS quality bits, performs subtraction and aperture photometry, combines repeat visits and builds light curves. A seven-endpoint API serves images, metadata and spectra with a disk cache. The web interface plays it all back.

The one fact the whole design follows

SPHEREx is not a camera with filters. The filter varies continuously along each detector, so a single exposure measures the target at one wavelength that depends on where it landed on the array. There is no “image of band 29” to download — a spectrum must be assembled from many exposures taken at different times. We confirmed this on real data: six consecutive D2 exposures of R Draconis landed in bands 28 through 33, one per channel.

Benefits: the errors that never raise an error

The SPHEREx archive is public and free, but it punishes reasonable assumptions silently:

  • The published coordinates for WISE 0855-0714 date from around 2010. Used as they are, they miss the object by 21 pixels. You measure empty sky and get a number back.
  • FLAGS bit 21 is SOURCE, the source mask, not a defect. Masking everything flagged leaves 0 usable pixels out of 841 — it erases the object you came to measure.
  • Frames at different wavelengths are indistinguishable in a file listing. Subtracting two of them produces a clean, meaningless residual.
  • Bands overlap at the seams between detectors, so a band must be chosen within a single detector or you silently mix optics.

None of these throw an exception. Each returns a plausible, wrong answer. The viewer makes the correct choice the default and labels every frame ok, suspect or bad, with the reason in plain language.

Intended impact

To move the cost of a first look at SPHEREx data from weeks of reading documentation to opening a web page. For students, teachers and amateur astronomers, it is a way to see a real survey behave like a survey — the same object, many nights, many wavelengths. For researchers it is triage: decide in a minute whether a position is worth a serious reduction.

What it already produces is measured, not claimed: RW Aurigae varies by a factor of 7.6 across 8 epochs; two epochs of Epsilon Indi B taken 525 days apart leave a 72σ dipole; R Draconis saturates. That last one cost us something. We had recommended R Draconis as our best photometry case because it has 222 observation dates, then found the BLOOM and HALO flags and withdrew our own recommendation in the documentation. We would rather ship a correct “no” than an attractive “yes”.

Tools, languages and software

  • Science core — Python 3.11 with numpy, astropy and pyyaml. Pure functions: arrays in, arrays or dictionaries out, no network and no disk, so every scientific claim is testable in isolation.
  • Backend — FastAPI, httpx, scipy and pillow. Seven endpoints, a disk cache, and every IRSA call routed through a single module with retries and backoff.
  • Frontend — Vite, React and TypeScript, with Aladin Lite (CDS, Strasbourg) for sky context. Fully bilingual, English and Spanish.
  • Testing and CI — 307 automated tests (169 Python, 138 frontend) run by GitHub Actions on every push and pull request.
  • NASA data and resources — IRSA’s TAP service (spherex.plane, spherex.artifact, spherex.obscore), IRSA’s cutout service for original FITS MEF files, and IRSA’s HiPS mirror for 2MASS, AllWISE and DSS2 sky context. The meaning of every FLAGS quality bit is transcribed from Table 16 of the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement (SSDC-DP-017 v2.0), published by IRSA. None of it was guessed.
  • Hardware — ordinary laptops. The site runs on free hosting tiers; no GPUs and no special equipment.

How it is creative

Archives present a survey as a list of files. We made time the primary axis: the same sky, playing. The second idea is less obvious — we designed the product around the traps rather than around the features. Most tools expose what the data offers; this one is built to stop you from getting a wrong answer that looks right. Third, the URL is the unit of sharing, so a finding travels as a link that reconstructs the exact view. And we put our own negative results inside the product, where a user making the same mistake will actually read them.

Factors the team considered

IRSA is a shared public service, so all access goes through one module, capped at 8 concurrent connections, with retries and backoff, and the four example targets are precomputed so that a demonstration never depends on a live query. That decision proved itself while we prepared this submission: IRSA’s TAP service returned HTTP 502 and the precomputed targets kept working.

Free hosting shaped the design too — FITS downloads redirect to IRSA rather than proxying megabytes through our own server. We were careful not to promise resolution we do not have: the two brown dwarfs of Epsilon Indi B are 0.72 arcseconds apart and a SPHEREx pixel is 6.2 arcseconds, so they appear as a single source and the interface says exactly that. Zodiacal light is supplied by the pipeline but not subtracted, and we say so rather than quietly removing it.

Finally, the deployed site serves no sample data. Everything on screen comes from IRSA at request time.
